profile.summary: GENEB compares 40 genomic foundation models on 100 DNA sequence classification tasks in 13 functional categories, such as promoters, enhancers, histone marks, DNA methylation and splice sites. Every model is scored the same way: a logistic-regression probe trained on frozen sequence embeddings, in full-data, 10-shot and 1-shot regimes, with MCC as the main metric. It is meant for choosing a DNA model for a particular kind of task rather than for a single overall ranking.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: opening paragraphs and Benchmark table; Paper: Abstract

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: GENEB tests how much task-relevant information a pretrained DNA model's frozen embeddings carry. Tasks are binary or multi-class sequence classification problems in 13 categories: histone modifications (30 tasks), promoters (22), enhancers (8), DNA methylation (8), splice sites (7), lncRNA (6), mouse enhancers (5), TF binding (5), species classification (3), regulatory elements (2), virus or phage (2), coding versus non-coding (1) and chromatin accessibility (1). The authors argue that rankings change across categories and data regimes, so results are reported per task and per category as well as overall.
sections.source_locator: benchmark_spec.json: categories; README.md: opening note

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The tasks are taken from nine earlier benchmark collections: the original and revised Nucleotide Transformer tasks, GUE, Genomic Benchmarks, the Plant Genomic Benchmark, iPro-WAEL, deep4mc, iDNA-ABF and iDHS-EL. Each task is one CSV with a sequence, a label and a train or test split. The released train and test partitions of the source benchmarks are used as published, without relabelling or resplitting. Tasks with more than 10^5 sequences are subsampled. The task data are pinned to one Hugging Face dataset revision in benchmark_spec.json.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Appendix B; README.md: Evaluation protocol; benchmark_spec.json: dataset

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: A submission is an embedding extractor that turns each DNA sequence into one fixed-length vector. The harness fits a logistic-regression probe (max_iter=1000) on the training embeddings and scores the test set, in three regimes: all training data, 10 examples per class and 1 example per class. Results are averaged over five fixed seeds (13, 17, 42, 123, 997). MCC is the primary metric; accuracy and macro-F1 are also reported. The leaderboard gives a micro average over all 100 tasks and a macro average, the unweighted mean of the 13 category scores. Encoders must not be fine-tuned on task labels. Evaluation is run by the contributor; continuous integration checks the submission file but does not recompute embeddings, and community entries are marked self-reported.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Section 3 Probing setup; README.md: Evaluation protocol, Leaderboard; run_GENEB.py: few_shot_idx; CONTRIBUTING.md: What CI verifies

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: Download the pinned task data with the repository's sync tool, write an extractor class for your model under harness/extractors/, run harness/run_GENEB.py (the README suggests --limit 5 for a smoke test) and validate the submission file it writes. The README commands use placeholder names for the extractor and model.

strengths.text: Every model is run on the full task suite under one probe protocol, which the authors say allows matched comparisons across architecture, tokenisation and pretraining data.
Results are reported per task and per category, and in three data regimes, not only as one aggregate.
The task data revision is pinned in the benchmark definition, and the harness, submissions and leaderboard build are public.

limitations.text: Results are self-reported: maintainers do not re-run submissions, and CI only checks the file format and ranges.
Splits are inherited from the source benchmarks and no check for overlap with pretraining data is made, so some models may have seen test sequences during pretraining.

profile.summary: This is the human variant effect evaluation in the Evo 2 paper, not a released benchmark suite. The authors scored ClinVar variants, SpliceVarDB splice variants and BRCA1 and BRCA2 functional assay variants zero-shot with Evo 2 and a range of comparison models, and report AUROC and AUPRC per variant stratum. It is useful for seeing how a DNA language model compares with conservation scores, protein language models and supervised predictors on coding, noncoding, SNV and non-SNV variants.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Human variant effect prediction, Fig. 3 legend; SI: A.3.12 to A.3.15

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether a model's zero-shot score separates harmful from harmless human variants. Four label sources are used: ClinVar pathogenic or likely pathogenic versus benign or likely benign; SpliceVarDB experimentally validated splice-altering variants; BRCA1 saturation genome editing classes (loss of function versus functional or intermediate); and BRCA2 functional classifications. ClinVar results are split into coding and noncoding, SNV and non-SNV, by phyloP conservation bin and by distance from splice sites, so the evaluation also covers insertions, deletions and other non-SNVs that many predictors cannot score.
sections.source_locator: SI: A.3.13 to A.3.15; Paper: Human variant effect prediction

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: ClinVar is the October 2024 release, restricted to nuclear variants with at least two review stars, with variants of unknown significance removed and variants affecting more than 64 bp of reference or alternate sequence removed. SpliceVarDB variants labelled low frequency are excluded. BRCA1 and BRCA2 labels are the classes assigned in the original assay studies: for BRCA1, 823 loss-of-function SNVs against 3,070 functional or intermediate SNVs; for BRCA2, 1,156 against 5,681. All models score the same variants within each benchmark.

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Each variant is scored zero-shot as the change in log-likelihood between the variant and reference sequence; a more negative change means more deleterious. Evo 2 scores an 8,192 bp genomic window around the variant. Encoder models use masked marginal likelihood for SNVs and the change in pseudolikelihood for non-SNVs; PhyloP non-SNV scores average the affected positions; Pangolin uses the largest absolute predicted change in splice site usage. Classification is scored with AUROC and AUPRC per stratum. The full per-model, per-stratum results are in Supplementary Data 1. A separate supervised BRCA1 experiment trains ridge regression on Evo 2 embeddings with a position-grouped 80/20 split; it is not part of the zero-shot comparison.

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: ClinVar October 2024 (coding: 14,319 SNVs and 1,236 non-SNVs; noncoding: 34,761 SNVs and 3,894 non-SNVs), SpliceVarDB (1,181 exonic and 3,769 intronic variants), BRCA1 saturation genome editing SNVs (3,893; 2,077 coding and 1,125 noncoding) and BRCA2 functional SNVs (1,156 loss of function and 5,681 functional or intermediate).

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: No train or test split for the zero-shot comparison: all variants are evaluation data. The separate supervised BRCA1 experiment splits 1,326 genomic positions 80/20 into 3,104 training and 789 test SNVs.

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: AUROC and AUPRC per stratum; higher is better.

facts.label: Baselines

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: No variant-level control is described for comparison models. For Evo 2, the authors state it was not trained on human genetic variation or functional genomics data. Supervised comparators such as CADD, SpliceAI and Pangolin may have been trained on overlapping labels; the sources do not address this.

Within each benchmark all models score the same variants, and ClinVar results are stratified by conservation and splice-site distance.
Uses functional assay labels (BRCA1, BRCA2, SpliceVarDB) alongside clinical labels.

No scoring code for the full comparison is listed in the availability statements, only the Evo 2 repository with an example BRCA1 notebook. Supplementary Data 1 is described as scores and metadata for the human variant effect prediction analysis; it was not read for this page.

profile.summary: This paper evaluates 21 RNA language models, with DNA language models as reference controls, on three zero-shot tasks: secondary structure prediction from attention maps, RNA family and type classification from embedding similarity, and mutational fitness prediction from sequence likelihoods. No model is fine-tuned. It helps researchers judge what structural, functional and evolutionary information a pretrained RNA model carries before choosing one.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Each task reads a different part of the model. Secondary structure prediction reads attention weights, RNA classification reads embeddings, and fitness prediction reads token-level logits. Together they test whether a model has learned base pairing, functional similarity between RNAs, and the effect of mutations, without any task training.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Key Points; Data and methods

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Secondary structure labels are base pairs from experimentally resolved 3D structures: a validation set VL1 (40 PDBs) and a test set TS (70 PDBs) curated in earlier work, with sequence identity below 80% and TM-score below 0.45 between them, and a TS-Hard subset (15 PDBs) with no shared Rfam family. RfamSample takes 10 sequences from each Rfam 14.0 family with more than 10 members, giving 561 families. ArchiveII-Nr is ArchiveII reduced with MMseqs2 at 80% identity to 1273 RNAs. Fitness uses 31 ncRNA deep mutational scanning assays from RNAGym with wild-type length up to 440 nucleotides. Models were included if released before 1 August 2025 with open weights; each task uses the models whose attention, embeddings or logits were available.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Data and methods, Datasets

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Structure: attention maps from every head and layer are symmetrised, corrected with average product correction and passed through a sigmoid; one head-layer and threshold are chosen on VL1 by F1 and applied unchanged to TS and TS-Hard, scored by MCC and F1. Classification: embeddings are reduced to fixed length with a Fourier transform (FFT) or taken from the CLS token, and cosine similarities of homologous and non-homologous pairs are compared by MCC, AUC and the overlap ratio (OR), reported as 1 - OR so that higher is better; 100,000 homologous and 100,000 non-homologous pairs are sampled from RfamSample. Fitness: variants are scored by wild-type conditioned log-likelihood ratio (WT-LLR) or pseudo-log-likelihood difference (PLL-D) and compared with assay values by MCC, AUC and absolute Spearman correlation. Metrics are averaged over repeated random samplings where applicable.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Zero-shot evaluation; Statistical analysis; Results

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: Download bib.zip from the Zenodo record, then in each task folder run the shell scripts and combine results with metric.py. The authors note that each language model needs its own Python environment and model path, set by the user, and that the scripts are an example for reference.
sections.source_locator: ReadMe.md

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: VL1 (40 PDBs), TS (70 PDBs) and TS-Hard (15 PDBs) for structure; RfamSample (561 families) and ArchiveII-Nr (1273 RNAs) for classification; 31 RNAGym ncRNA DMS assays for fitness.

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: Structure uses VL1 to choose the head-layer and threshold and TS or TS-Hard to test. Classification and fitness have no training split: all data are evaluation data.

facts.label: Metrics

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: DNA language models as reference controls: DNABERT for structure; DNABERT, DNABERT-2 and NT among others for classification and fitness.

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: For structure, VL1 and TS share under 80% sequence identity and TM-score under 0.45, and TS-Hard removes shared Rfam families. Overlap between test RNAs and model pretraining data is not checked.

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: Classification metrics are means over repeated random samplings of pairs and some are given with a standard deviation (for example 1 - OR = 0.878 ± 0.001 for RNA-FM). Structure and fitness results are reported as medians or means across structures or assays.

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: Structure: an RNA sequence with a base-pair map. Classification: a pair of RNA sequences. Fitness: a mutant RNA sequence with a measured effect.

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Unreported as a list: the datasets are drawn from PDB, Rfam, ArchiveII and RNAGym across many species.

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: Experimentally resolved 3D RNA structures for structure labels, Rfam and ArchiveII annotations for classification, and deep mutational scanning for fitness.

facts.label: Adaptation

strengths.text: One protocol per task, applied to 21 RNA models and DNA controls, with code and data released on Zenodo under CC BY 4.0.
The structure test includes a homology-excluded TS-Hard set; the authors report a Spearman correlation of 0.99 between median MCC rankings on TS and TS-Hard.
Tests three separate model outputs (attention, embeddings, logits), so a model's strengths can be compared across them.

limitations.text: Test sets are small: TS-Hard has 15 structures, and the authors refer to its limited size.
Models are included in a task only where their attention, embeddings or logits are available, so the model set differs between tasks.
The run scripts need per-model environments and model paths set by the user; the authors call them an example for reference.
The data availability statement links to Zenodo record 14430869 but prints record 18218776; the two are different versions of the deposit.

profile.summary: ViroBench tests nucleotide foundation models on viral sequences from NCBI. Its classification half asks a model to predict a virus's taxonomy (Kingdom to Family) and its host category, under two hard splits: one that holds out whole genera and one that splits by deposit date. Models are compared with a frozen backbone and a small trained head, scored by macro-F1, precision, recall and AUPRC. It is for anyone judging how a DNA or RNA model generalises to viruses it has not seen.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract, Section 3; README.md: Benchmark Suite

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Two classification tasks. Taxonomy classification predicts five hierarchical labels from Kingdom to Family, testing whether a model's representation reflects viral evolutionary structure. Host prediction assigns a sequence to one of eight coarse host categories, testing whether the representation carries ecological signal. Each task is run on the whole viral corpus (ALL) and separately on the DNA and RNA subsets, under both splits, giving 12 classification scenarios. The paper also defines six generation scenarios on a second axis, which this page does not cover.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Section 3.2.1; README.md: Benchmark Suite

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The authors retrieved 273,974 virus-associated TaxIDs from NCBI RefSeq and GenBank and recorded taxonomy, the earliest discovery date and host for each. Raw host metadata, over 8,000 inconsistent strings, was standardised into eight coarse categories using the Qwen3-235B language model. Entries with incomplete taxonomy or missing timestamps were removed, only verified high-quality assemblies were kept, and species-level redundancy was resolved, leaving 58,314 samples. Two split protocols are defined over the same data: a genus-disjoint split with no genus shared between train, validation and test, and a temporal split by deposit date with stated cutoffs per panel (for example 2017.10 and 2020.02 for the ALL set). Both use an 8:1:1 train, validation and test ratio.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Section 3.1, Table 1

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: The backbone is frozen: sequence embeddings are precomputed with each model's own pooling strategy and a lightweight multi-task classification head is trained on them. Long sequences are handled by windowing, with 8, 4 or 2 windows sampled per sequence during training; at validation and test time all windows are scored and aggregated into one sequence-level prediction. Learning rates from 10^-2 to 10^-4 and the different window configurations are tried, and results are reported as the mean with standard deviation across those settings. Metrics are AUPRC, recall, precision and macro-F1, chosen for the class imbalance. A CNN trained from scratch is the non-pretrained reference.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Section 4.1, Appendix frozen-backbone protocol; README.md: Unified Evaluation Protocol

The dataset itself is downloaded from the Hugging Face repository. The README says model-specific setup must follow each model's own documentation.

facts.value: One curated corpus of 58,314 viral samples from NCBI RefSeq and GenBank, used as ALL, DNA and RNA panels. Table 1 gives the label counts per panel, for example 29 / 55 / 214 / 390 / 319 labels at Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order and Family for ALL viruses.

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: Two protocols over the same data, both 8:1:1 train, validation and test. Genus-disjoint: no genus appears in more than one partition. Temporal: split by deposit date, with per-panel cutoffs (ALL 2017.10 and 2020.02; DNA 2022.07 and 2023.08; RNA 2017.03 and 2017.11).

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Macro-F1 is the headline classification metric (Table 25); AUPRC, recall and precision are also reported. Higher is better.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Section 4.1, Table 25 caption; README.md: Metrics

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: 66 nucleotide foundation models plus 4 conventional baselines, 70 methods in total; the paper names BLAST, Kraken2, a BiLSTM and a CNN trained from scratch among the conventional ones. The README says 67 baselines.

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: The genus-disjoint split removes genus overlap between partitions, which the authors describe as mandating phylogenetic extrapolation; the temporal split holds out later deposits. Overlap between test sequences and a model's own pretraining data is not controlled.

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: Means with standard deviations across the learning rate and window configurations tried, as stated in the Table 25 caption and the setup.

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: One viral nucleotide sequence from an NCBI record, with taxonomy, deposit date and host metadata.

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Viruses, split into DNA, RNA and unknown nucleic-acid types; host labels cover eight coarse categories such as bacterial, plant and human.

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: Inapplicable: labels are database annotations (NCBI taxonomy, deposit dates and host metadata standardised by a language model), not experimental measurements.

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: Nucleotide sequence only, read through each model's own tokeniser and pooling; sequences longer than a model's context are windowed.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Appendix, Embedding Extraction and Pooling

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Frozen backbone with a lightweight supervised head for classification; no fine-tuning of the pretrained weights.

strengths.text: Both splits are harder than a random split: one removes whole genera, the other holds out later deposits, so memorised near-duplicates do not inflate scores.
All models go through the same frozen-backbone protocol with a standard head, which the authors say reduces bias from different tokenisers and architectures.
Results are reported with standard deviations over learning rates and window settings rather than a single tuned number.

limitations.text: Host prediction is a single label over coarse categories, using the primary-host annotation; the authors say a multi-label version is future work.
The temporal split uses NCBI deposit dates, which the authors say reflect sequencing intensity rather than when a virus actually emerged.
Host labels were standardised from over 8,000 inconsistent strings by a language model (Qwen3-235B), so label quality depends on that step.
The repository carries no licence file, and the model counts differ between the paper (66 models, 70 methods) and the README (67 baselines).

profile.summary: This is the third edition of the Livesey and Marsh benchmark of missense variant effect predictors. It ranks 97 predictors by how well their scores correlate with deep mutational scanning measurements in 36 human proteins, and separately ranks 83 predictors by how well they separate ClinVar pathogenic from gnomAD population missense variants in 819 proteins. Rankings are pairwise: each predictor's score is its average win rate against every other predictor on the variants both of them score.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Results, Fig. 2 and Fig. 3 legends

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Two things. First, agreement between a predictor's scores and experimental fitness measurements from deep mutational scanning, using absolute Spearman correlation, because only a monotonic relationship is needed. Second, discrimination between pathogenic and population missense variants in clinical data, using AUROC per protein. The authors' premise is that a predictor consistent across many functional assays is the most useful one, and they report that relative performance on the assay benchmark predicts relative performance on the clinical one for predictors not trained on human clinical variants.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Results, Comparison of VEP performance using DMS data; Abstract

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The assay set starts from the 26 datasets of the previous edition, removes every variant also present in the authors' ClinVar and gnomAD sets, then keeps only datasets with at least 1000 scored amino acid variants. Datasets measuring antibody binding or unrelated binding affinity, and those without methodological details, were excluded; 13 new datasets, mostly from MaveDB, were added, giving 36 proteins and 207,460 single amino acid variants. One score set per protein is used, chosen as the one with the highest median Spearman correlation across all predictors. The clinical set takes ClinVar missense variants (downloaded 06/08/2024) labelled pathogenic, likely pathogenic or pathogenic/likely pathogenic, drops 0-star entries and entries with conflicting interpretations, and uses gnomAD v4.1 missense variants that pass the genomes or exomes filters as a putatively benign class. Proteins with at least 10 of each class qualify, giving 819 proteins.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods; Results, New DMS datasets and VEPs; Performance of VEPs on clinical variant classification

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: For each protein, the absolute Spearman correlation with the assay is computed for every pair of predictors using only variants all three (assay and both predictors) score. The predictor with the higher correlation wins the comparison. Win rates are pooled over proteins and the rank score is the average win rate against all other predictors. The clinical ranking uses the same pairwise procedure with AUROC in place of Spearman, and a parallel version uses AUPRC. Predictors that score low for pathogenic are inverted by subtracting from 1. Error bars on the assay ranking are the standard deviation of the rank score over 1000 bootstraps resampling 36 protein datasets with replacement; error bars on the clinical ranking are the standard error across comparisons.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Spearman's correlation and rank score; AUROC and AUPRC; Fig. 2 and Fig. 3 legends

facts.value: No train, validation or test split: all data are evaluation data, and the predictors are external tools. Variants present in ClinVar or gnomAD are removed from the assay benchmark, and datasets were excluded for predictors trained on that assay data.

strengths.text: Pairwise comparison on shared variants removes the advantage a predictor could gain from scoring only an easy subset, which the authors show can otherwise produce outliers.

Predictions, clinical labels and the analysis scripts are deposited on figshare, the data under CC BY 4.0 and the scripts under MIT.

limitations.text: A rank score is relative, not absolute: it depends on which other predictors are in the comparison and is not a correlation or an AUROC.

limitations.text: The negative class is gnomAD population variants, which the authors accept will contain some pathogenic variants not yet classified, especially in recessive and incompletely penetrant genes.
Each protein is represented by one assay score set, chosen as the one correlating best with the predictors on average, so the choice depends on the predictors being tested.

profile.summary: This is the human genome annotation evaluation from the SegmentNT paper. A model must label every nucleotide of a DNA sequence with 14 types of genomic element, from protein-coding genes and exons to splice sites, promoters, enhancers and CTCF-bound sites. Performance is measured per element and per nucleotide, as MCC and area under the precision-recall curve on held-out chromosomes 20 and 21. It is used to compare segmentation models and architectures on how precisely they place genomic features.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Results and Methods; Supplementary Tables 2 and 3 captions

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Per-nucleotide localisation of 14 element types, split into gene elements (protein-coding genes, lncRNAs, 5' UTR, 3' UTR, exon, intron, splice acceptor and donor sites) and regulatory elements (poly(A) signal, tissue-invariant and tissue-specific promoters and enhancers, CTCF-bound sites). Each element is a separate binary mask over the sequence, so a model is judged on each element in turn rather than on one combined score.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Human genomic elements; Results

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Gene elements and poly(A) signals come from GENCODE V44, filtered to drop level three (automated) transcripts so every training annotation is human-curated; introns and splice sites were extracted with the HISAT2 script. Promoters, enhancers and CTCF-bound sites come from ENCODE's SCREEN database, with distal and proximal enhancers combined and each promoter or enhancer labelled tissue-invariant or tissue-specific using the Meuleman et al. vocabulary. The dataset is built by overlapping all 14 element tracks with every DNA sequence of the chosen length; sequences containing N are removed.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Human genomic elements

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: The split is by chromosome: chromosomes 20 and 21 are the test set, chromosome 22 is validation and the rest is training. Test chunks containing genes homologous to genes on the training or validation chromosomes were removed using Ensembl BioMart annotations (accessed 8 May 2024). Validation and test sequences are fixed by sliding a window of the model's length over the chromosome. A model outputs 14 probabilities per nucleotide; the predictions are concatenated across sequences per element type and scored per nucleotide with MCC, auPRC, Jaccard similarity and F1, plus a region-level SOV score. The test set was sampled ten times with different window start positions to give a spread. The best checkpoint is chosen on the validation chromosome by average MCC over the 14 elements.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Model training and evaluation; Supplementary Table 2 caption

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: The repository ships inference code in Jax. Clone it, install the package, then load a pretrained segmentation model with get_pretrained_segment_nt_model, tokenise sequences and read the per-nucleotide probabilities for each of the 14 features. The published evaluation itself, including the test chromosome manifests, is not released as a script.
sections.source_locator: README.md: installation; docs/segment_nt.md: How to use

strengths.text: Every element is scored separately at nucleotide resolution, so a model's strength on, say, splice sites is visible rather than averaged away.
The split is by chromosome and test chunks with genes homologous to training genes are removed, which is stricter than a random split.

strengths.text: Ten test samplings give a standard deviation for every reported number, and ablations include randomly initialised and head-only models.

limitations.text: Homologous distal regulatory elements are not removed from the test set, which the authors say could still inflate performance in those regions.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Model training and evaluation

limitations.text: There is no released evaluation harness or test manifest: the repository gives inference code, not the benchmark pipeline, so another group cannot reproduce the exact test set from the sources read.

steps.title: Run the model on sequences
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
import haiku as hk
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
from nucleotide_transformer.pretrained import get_pretrained_segment_nt_model

jax.config.update("jax_platform_name", "cpu")
backend = "cpu"
devices = jax.devices(backend)
max_num_nucleotides = 8
parameters, forward_fn, tokenizer, config = get_pretrained_segment_nt_model(
    model_name="segment_nt",
    embeddings_layers_to_save=(29,),
    attention_maps_to_save=((1, 4), (7, 10)),
    max_positions=max_num_nucleotides + 1,
)
forward_fn = hk.transform(forward_fn)
apply_fn = jax.pmap(forward_fn.apply, devices=devices, donate_argnums=(0,))
sequences = ["ATTCCGATTCCGATTCCAACGGATTATTCCGATTAACCGATTCCAATT", "ATTTCTCTCTCTCTCTGAGATCGATGATTTCTCTCTCATCGAACTATG"]
tokens_ids = [b[1] for b in tokenizer.batch_tokenize(sequences)]
tokens = jnp.asarray(tokens_ids, dtype=jnp.int32)
random_key = jax.random.PRNGKey(seed=0)
keys = jax.device_put_replicated(random_key, devices=devices)
parameters = jax.device_put_replicated(parameters, devices=devices)
tokens = jax.device_put_replicated(tokens, devices=devices)
outs = apply_fn(parameters, keys, tokens)
logits = outs["logits"]
probabilities = jnp.asarray(jax.nn.softmax(logits, axis=-1))[...,-1]
print(f"Features inferred: {config.features}")
PY

profile.summary: This is a benchmark of taxonomic classification and profiling tools, not of models. Eleven methods, five of them written for long reads, were run on public mock community datasets sequenced with PacBio HiFi, Oxford Nanopore and Illumina, where the species present and their intended abundances are known. Each method is scored on how many reads it uses, how precisely and completely it detects the known species, and how close its abundance estimates are to the manufacturer's specification.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Materials and methods

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Three things per method and dataset. Read utilisation: what fraction of the reads the method assigns. Detection: precision, recall and F-score for the known species or genera, where a true positive is a mock community taxon whose read count passes a threshold and a false positive is any taxon not in the community. Abundance accuracy: the L1 distance between estimated and theoretical abundances, with a chi-squared goodness of fit test against the manufacturer's specification.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Materials and methods, Detection metrics and Relative abundance estimates

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The datasets are public, empirical sequencing runs of commercial mock communities, chosen over simulations because simulations do not capture real error profiles, read length spread or extraction and library effects. They include a PacBio HiFi run of ATCC MSA-1003 (20 bacterial species in staggered abundances from 18% down to 0.02%; 2.4 million HiFi reads, median length 8.3 kb, 20.54 Gb) and a PacBio HiFi run of ZymoBIOMICS D6331 (17 species including one archaeon and two yeasts, staggered from 14% down to 0.0001%; 1.9 million reads, median 8.1 kb, 17.99 Gb), plus Oxford Nanopore R10 and Q20 runs of ZymoBIOMICS D6300 and Illumina runs of both communities. The truth is the species list and the manufacturer's stated genomic DNA abundances.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Materials and methods, Mock community datasets; Relative abundance estimates

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Presence or absence is scored against a minimum percentage of the dataset's total reads, not a fixed read count, because the datasets differ in size. Three thresholds are used: 0.001% (mild), 0.1% (moderate) and 1% (heavy); Table 3 gives the resulting read counts per dataset, for example 24 reads at 0.001% and 24,190 at 1% for HiFi ATCC MSA-1003. Scoring is done at both species and genus level. Abundances are normalised with all false positives summed into an 'Other' category, which is compared against a theoretical abundance of zero, and the chi-squared test uses a Bonferroni correction over the 11 methods, so the altered alpha is 0.0045.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Materials and methods, Detection metrics; Relative abundance estimates; Table 3

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: The paper prints the general command for each method, so a reader can repeat the analysis on the same public datasets. Kraken2 2.1.1 with the pre-built PlusPF database writes a kreport per sample; Bracken 2.6.0 then produces species-level abundances from that kreport. The other methods each have their own commands and databases in the same section. The kreport outputs, notebooks and results files are on the Open Science Framework project bqtdu.

profile.summary: GFMBench-API is a Python interface that puts many existing genomic benchmarks behind one evaluation API. A model implements a small set of inference methods, and the library then runs it on 22 tasks covering supervised sequence and variant classification and zero-shot variant effect prediction, writing one CSV of task and metric rows. It is for comparing genomic foundation models without rewriting a pipeline per benchmark.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: opening, Supported Benchmarks & Tasks, Benchmark Output

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Two families of task. Supervised classification and variant prediction: promoter, splice site and transcription factor binding from GUE; coding, non-coding, expression, common versus rare, methylation QTL and splicing QTL variant classification from VariantBenchmarks; causal eQTL, enhancer and histone mark tasks from the Long Range Benchmark. Zero-shot variant effect prediction: ClinVar SNVs by embedding distance and by likelihood, ClinVar insertions and deletions, BEND expression and disease effects, BRCA1 functional impact, TraitGym complex and Mendelian variants, LRB pathogenic OMIM variants and LOL-EVE causal eQTL indels.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Supported Benchmarks & Tasks

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The tasks wrap data from existing benchmarks rather than new data collection. All task data sit under one root directory, one subdirectory per task named after the task class, holding train.csv, dev.csv and test.csv; missing files are downloaded automatically on first use. Classification data carry a sequence and a label; variant effect data carry a reference sequence, an alternative sequence and a label. Sequences use A, T, C, G, N and P for padding at chromosome boundaries, and are upper-cased. The NOTICE states that the downloaded third-party data include datasets with non-commercial terms.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Data Preparation; NOTICE

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: A model supplies inference methods by duck typing: sequence to label probabilities, variant and reference pairs to label probabilities, sequence to regression outputs, sequence to per-nucleotide probabilities and embeddings, a position mapping helper, and masked-position token probabilities. Any method a model does not implement can return None and the metrics that need it are skipped. Supervised classification tasks compute accuracy, MCC, AUROC and AUPRC. Zero-shot SNV tasks add cosine similarity AUROC and AUPRC between variant and reference embeddings at the variant position, and AUROC and AUPRC on the masked-token log-likelihood ratio. Tasks expose eval_test_set, eval_validation_set and eval_cross_validation_fold, and results go to a CSV with one row per task and metric and one column per model name, with NO_RESULTS where a result is missing.
sections.source_locator: README.md: How Model & Task Interfaces Work, Benchmark Output; base task classes

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: Install your model's own dependencies first, then the library's basic_requirements.txt on top, and run usage_examples/run_benchmark.py with a model key. Flags select linear probing, the number of fine-tuning epochs, the output CSV path and the inference cache size. A sanity check mode runs on 100-sample subsets. If a model's dependencies clash with the benchmark stack, the model can run in a separate Python environment and process behind a thin adapter.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Quick Start, Example: Running Benchmarks

profile.summary: These are the two clinical missense benchmarks from the ESM1b variant effect paper. One labels variants from ClinVar as pathogenic or benign; the other treats HGMD disease-causing variants as positives and gnomAD variants with allele frequency above 1% as negatives. Predictors are scored by a global ROC-AUC over all variants together, plus a class-balanced PRC-AUC, and only methods that avoid clinical-database training and allele frequency features are included in the main comparison.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Results, ESM1b outperforms other VEP methods; Methods, AUC metrics for pathogenicity classification

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether a variant effect predictor separates harmful from harmless missense variants across the whole genome, not within one gene. The authors argue a global score matters because diagnosis means comparing variants in different genes, so the scores must be comparable between genes; they also report the gene-average ROC-AUC used by the EVE paper for contrast.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, AUC metrics for pathogenicity classification

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: ClinVar labels come from ClinVar's variant summary file, with only high-confidence variants kept. In the ESM1b versus EVE comparison the ClinVar set has 19,925 pathogenic and 16,612 benign variants across 2,765 genes, and the HGMD and gnomAD set has 27,754 disease-causing and 2,743 common variants across 1,991 genes; the paper does not say whether the full sets are larger. A separate ClinVar benchmark with EVE scores came from the EVE portal. Predictions for most of the compared methods were downloaded from dbNSFP 4.3a, with VARITY and MTBAN added separately. HGMD is a private resource, so that half of the benchmark cannot be redistributed.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Results; Methods, Other VEP methods; Data availability; README.md: Data Availability

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Global ROC-AUC over the pooled variants is the main metric. The balanced PRC-AUC downsamples each dataset to an equal number of pathogenic and benign variants, taking 80% of the minority class, and averages over 100 such draws. Two comparison modes are reported: all 19 eligible methods on the variants that all of them score, and head-to-head comparisons where ESM1b is compared with each method on that method's own set of scored variants, with the percentage of variants used shown. Differences are tested by permutation, shuffling scores between variants over 2,000 iterations.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, AUC metrics and Testing for significant performance differences; Fig. 2 legend

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: The repository holds the processed benchmark files with every method's predictions, except the HGMD variants, plus command line tools that score missense or multi-residue mutations with ESM1b. Install the dependencies, clone the repository, then run esm_score_missense_mutations.py on a FASTA file to get a score for every possible missense mutation.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Repository Contents, Installation, Usage

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: Two sets, ClinVar and HGMD with gnomAD. The paper gives counts for the variants in the ESM1b versus EVE comparison (Fig. 2b): ClinVar, 19,925 pathogenic and 16,612 benign missense variants in 2,765 genes (36,537 in total); HGMD and gnomAD, 27,754 disease-causing and 2,743 common variants in 1,991 genes (30,497 in total). The paper does not state whether the full sets are larger.

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: No split: both sets are evaluation data only, and the compared predictors are external published methods.

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Global ROC-AUC across all variants pooled (higher is better) and a class-balanced PRC-AUC averaged over 100 downsamplings (higher is better). A gene-average ROC-AUC is reported for contrast.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, AUC metrics for pathogenicity classification

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: 46 variant effect predictors were collected, mostly from dbNSFP 4.3a, with VARITY (two versions) and MTBAN added. Of these, 19 including ESM1b and EVE qualify for the clinical benchmarks. LINSIGHT and three cell-line versions of fitCons were excluded.

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: Eligibility rules rather than data filtering: a method may enter the clinical comparison only if it was not trained on clinical databases such as ClinVar or HGMD, does not use features from methods trained on such data, and does not use allele frequency, since allele frequency is used to curate variants as benign. Results for the excluded methods are still reported in Supplementary Table 2.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results; Methods, Other VEP methods

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: The balanced PRC-AUC is averaged over 100 downsamplings. Differences between methods are tested by permutation over 2,000 iterations, reported as P < 0.001 when no permutation reaches the observed difference. Bootstrapped means and standard deviations are used for the stop-gain analysis, not for the missense benchmarks.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, AUC metrics; Testing for significant performance differences

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: A missense variant on a curated human protein isoform, labelled pathogenic or benign.

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Human.

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: No assay: labels are clinical assertions from ClinVar and HGMD, and population allele frequency from gnomAD. The paper's separate deep mutational scanning benchmark, which does use assays, is a different evaluation.

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: Whatever each published predictor uses; for the clinical comparison, methods using allele frequency features are excluded. ESM1b itself reads the protein sequence only, with a sliding window for long proteins.

facts.label: Adaptation

profile.summary: This is a Rewire-built calibration benchmark, not a published suite. It takes precomputed scores from eight variant predictors and foundation models and converts them into ACMG/AMP computational evidence thresholds (PP3 and BP4, from +1 to +8 and -1 to -8) using the Pejaver et al. 2022 local posterior method with the Bergquist et al. 2025 additions. The scoring set is ClinVar GRCh38 missense SNVs with at least two review stars that were not classified P/LP or B/LB in the 26 December 2023 ClinVar release (or the 30 March 2025 release for the sensitivity cohort). It runs on CPU from committed score tables.

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Two things at once. First, how well each predictor separates pathogenic or likely pathogenic from benign or likely benign missense variants, reported as AUROC with a 95% interval and AUPRC. Second, and the point of the exercise, which ACMG/AMP evidence strengths each predictor's scores can actually support: the score value at which the local posterior probability of pathogenicity reaches the cutoff for supporting, moderate, intermediate, strong and very strong evidence, in both directions. Where a predictor's scores never reach a strength on a cohort, the table records that it was not reached.

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Variants come from the ClinVar GRCh38 VCF of 8 November 2026, restricted to clean missense SNVs with at least two review stars. Three cohorts are drawn. post_2023_12 is the primary one: 9,450 variants (5,508 pathogenic or likely pathogenic, 3,942 benign or likely benign), of which 4,188 are new since 26 December 2023, excluding every variant already classified P/LP or B/LB in the December 2023 release. post_2023_12_af001 restricts the same cohort to 8,141 variants whose gnomAD v3.1.2 non-1000G genome grpmax frequency is below 0.1%. post_2025_03 is a sensitivity cohort of 3,818 variants held out from 30 March 2025. A separate population reference set of 6,312 missense SNVs (5,155 ClinVar variants of uncertain significance with population frequency and 1,157 gnomAD background SNVs), disjoint from the evaluation cohorts, supplies the population term the calibration needs.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Method, Temporal holdouts; cohort_summary.json; download_manifest.json

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: The calibration uses a disease prior alpha of 0.0441, c of 1124, a minimum of 100 points per local window and a population reference fraction gft of 0.03, following Pejaver et al. 2022. Bergquist et al. 2025 adds the +3 and -3 intermediate strengths and one-sided 95% conservative discounted thresholds from 1,000 bootstrap resamples, with seed 20261123. The posterior cutoffs that define each strength are recorded in the output (for example 0.0999 for supporting and 0.6073 for strong). The run took 173.51 seconds on CPU, and the receipt records the hash of every input score table and every output file.

profile.summary: The Nucleotide Transformer benchmark is a set of 18 human genomic classification tasks: ten histone marks in K562, three promoter tasks, two enhancer tasks and three splice site tasks. Each is a small balanced dataset of short sequences with a fixed chromosome-based test split, scored by Matthews correlation coefficient under tenfold cross-validation. The paper uses it to compare DNA language models after probing or fine-tuning, and the data are published on Hugging Face with an interactive leaderboard.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Methods, Nucleotide Transformer downstream tasks; Supplementary Table 5; Hugging Face dataset record

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether a model's representation of a short DNA sequence carries the signal for a specific regulatory or structural feature. The ten epigenetic tasks ask whether a 1 kb sequence overlaps a histone mark peak in K562. The promoter tasks ask whether a 300 bp sequence contains a promoter, a TATA-box promoter or a promoter without a TATA box. The enhancer tasks ask whether a 400 bp sequence contains an enhancer, and in the multi-label version whether it is tissue-specific or tissue-invariant. The splice tasks ask whether a 600 bp sequence has an acceptor or donor site in the centre.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Nucleotide Transformer downstream tasks

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Histone marks come from ten ENCODE ChIP-seq narrowPeak files for K562, each identifier listed in the Methods. Promoters come from the Eukaryotic Promoter Database (29,598 regions, 3,065 of them TATA-box). Enhancers come from ENCODE SCREEN, with distal and proximal combined and tissue specificity from the Meuleman DHS index. Splice sites come from GENCODE V44, excluding level-3 automated annotations, extracted with the HISAT2 script. Sequences containing N are removed, each dataset is balanced by subsampling negatives to the number of positives, and the sets are then capped at 30,000 training and 3,000 validation and test examples so a new model can be benchmarked quickly. Supplementary Table 5 lists the resulting sizes per task, from 5,062 training sequences for Promoter non-TATA to 30,000 for most tasks.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods; Supplementary Table 5

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: The split is by chromosome: chromosomes 20 and 21 are the test set and the rest is training. Evaluation uses tenfold cross-validation on the training set, training ten times with a different tenth held out for validation and checkpoint selection, and evaluating every run on the same held-out test set; the median across the ten folds is the reported performance. The metric is binary or multi-class MCC. For a single number per model, the authors take the median MCC within each of the three task categories (chromatin profiles, regulatory elements and splicing) and then the mean of those three.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Dataset splits and performance evaluation

sections.title: Probing and fine-tuning
sections.body: The paper reports two ways of using a pretrained model. Probing stores embeddings from ten layers of the model and trains a downstream logistic regression or MLP on them, with a hyperparameter search of 100 trials guided by a Tree-structured Parzen Estimator and the same tenfold scheme; the authors say this produced 760,000 downstream models. Fine-tuning is parameter-efficient on the transformer part. A logistic regression on the tokenised sequence, before the transformer layers, is the raw baseline.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Probing

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: The task data are published as a Hugging Face dataset, the revised version released after peer review, which the dataset card recommends using in place of the older one. The paper gives no command line pipeline for a third party to score a model, and results are collected in an interactive leaderboard on Hugging Face Spaces.

profile.summary: GenBench is a benchmark suite and codebase for genomic foundation models. It gathers forty-three datasets covering coding regions, non-coding regions and genome architecture, split into short-range tasks (inputs under 1,000 bases) and long-range tasks, and runs ten models through the same fine-tuning framework. Tasks include sequence classification, token classification and regression, scored by accuracy, AUC-ROC, Pearson or Spearman correlation and mean squared error depending on the task.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract, Sections 3.1 to 3.4; README.md: Introduction

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: The suite is organised around three parts of the genome: the coding region, the non-coding region and genome architecture. Short-range tasks, with inputs under one thousand bases, cover enhancers, promoters, transcription factor binding, splice sites, epigenetic marks, open chromatin, species discrimination and SARS-CoV-2 variant classification. Long-range tasks cover splice site annotation, species classification, promoter prediction, bulk RNA expression across 218 tissue types and genomic structure prediction. The paper's stated aim is to see whether attention-based and convolution-based models differ in where they do well.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Sections 1, 3.2 and 3.3

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The datasets are taken from earlier published collections rather than created: the Genomic Benchmarks tasks (mouse enhancers, coding versus intergenomic, human versus worm, enhancers, regulatory regions, non-TATA promoters, open chromatin), the GUE tasks (promoters, transcription factor binding, splice sites, yeast epigenetic marks, SARS-CoV-2 variants), the GENA-LM long-range tasks (splice sites, promoters, Drosophila enhancer activity), genomic structure prediction from Orca and species classification from HyenaDNA. Table 2 lists each task's type, training and test size and input length, from 30 bases for transcription factor prediction up to 256 Mb for genomic structure. For practicality the authors limited genomic structure prediction to 6,000 bases and capped long sequence tasks at 30 kb in their own experiments.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Sections 3.3 and 4, Table 2; README.md: supported datasets

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Models are fine-tuned within the suite's own framework, which loads pretrained weights from Hugging Face, so every model goes through the same pipeline. Metrics are chosen per task: cross-entropy as the error for classification and mean squared error for regression; top-1 accuracy and AUC-ROC for classification; Spearman and Pearson correlation for regression. Parameter count and floating point operations are also reported as computational measures. The published tables report top-1 accuracy for the short-range tasks, AUC-ROC for long-range splice site prediction, Pearson for Drosophila enhancer activity and genomic structure, and Spearman with MSE for bulk RNA expression.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Sections 3.4, 3.5 and 4, Tables 3 to 8

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: The codebase is organised into a core layer, an algorithm layer and a user interface layer, with configuration files per experiment. Create the conda environment from the shipped file, install the package, then run train.py with an experiment configuration, a dataset name and the path to a pretrained model. Each supported dataset has its own download link and configuration directory in the README.

facts.value: Forty-three datasets, grouped in Table 2 into twenty-one benchmark tasks: eight Genomic Benchmarks tasks at 500 bases, eight GUE and DeepSTARR short-range tasks from 30 to 256 bases, and five long-range tasks (splice site prediction at 15 kb, species classification at 80 Mb, promoters prediction at 8 kb, genomic structure at 256 Mb and bulk RNA expression at 196 kb). facts.value: Per task: top-1 accuracy and AUC-ROC for classification (higher is better), Pearson and Spearman correlation for regression (higher is better), and cross-entropy or mean squared error as the error metric (lower is better). Parameter count and FLOPs are reported alongside.

facts.value: Ten models: four attention-based (DNABERT, Nucleotide Transformer, DNABERT-2, GENA-LM) and six convolution-based or task-specific (HyenaDNA, Caduceus, a CNN, SpliceAI, DeepSTARR, Orca). The last four are trained from scratch with one-hot encoding as expert comparisons.

facts.value: None described. The paper does not state any identity cut-off, time split or held-out family, and does not check overlap between task data and model pretraining data.

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: Unextracted: the checklist states error bars were reported with respect to the random seed, but the result tables read print single values without intervals.

facts.value: A DNA sequence, with a class label for classification tasks or a continuous target for regression; splice site prediction and genomic structure prediction are scored per token or per position.

facts.value: Human, mouse, Drosophila, yeast, worm and SARS-CoV-2, as the task names indicate.

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: Varies by source dataset and is not described per task. The paper states that bulk RNA sequencing measures average gene expression across a group of cells in a tissue, and that Drosophila enhancer activity is two measured scores, housekeeping and developmental.

facts.value: DNA sequence only, as A, G, C, T or N, tokenised by each model's own tokeniser (k-mer, byte pair encoding, character or one-hot).

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Fine-tuning: pretrained weights are loaded and the model is trained on each downstream task within the suite's framework. The expert baselines are trained from scratch.

strengths.text: Covers both short and long inputs, with tasks up to the hundreds of kilobases, which the authors say earlier benchmarks either avoided or reduced to classification.
All ten models run through one modular codebase with per-experiment configuration files, released under Apache 2.0.
Task types go beyond classification to token-level classification and regression, including two-value regression for Drosophila enhancer activity and 218-dimensional bulk RNA output.

limitations.text: The authors state GenBench covers only downstream task prediction, with no comparison of pretraining choices, and that they did not test whole-chromosome performance because of compute limits.

Sequence lengths were cut for practicality: genomic structure prediction was limited to 6,000 bases and long sequence tasks were capped at 30 kb, so the stated input lengths in Table 2 are not what was run.
No leakage control is described, so a model pretrained on the human genome may have seen the test sequences as unlabelled data.
Some test sets are very small: three examples for genomic structure prediction, 242 for mouse enhancers and 500 for species classification.

profile.summary: TraitGym tests whether a model can pick out causal non-coding single-nucleotide variants in the human genome. It has two datasets: causal variants for 113 Mendelian traits and strong causal candidates for 83 complex traits, each paired with matched control variants. It is for people comparing DNA language models, sequence-to-function models and conservation or integrative scores on regulatory variant interpretation.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: The task is binary classification: is a variant putatively causal for any trait or not. Only non-coding single-nucleotide variants are included, because the authors see interpretation of non-coding variants as a key use for DNA sequence models. A model sees the reference and alternate alleles and the surrounding DNA sequence.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Section 4, Benchmark datasets and Task definition

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Mendelian positives are causal non-coding variants for 113 Mendelian diseases from OMIM, with variants above 0.1% minor allele frequency in gnomAD removed; common gnomAD variants are the controls. Complex-trait positives come from statistical fine-mapping of UK Biobank association studies: variants with posterior inclusion probability above 0.9 in any trait. Each positive is matched to 9 controls on chromosome, consequence and distance to the transcription start site; complex-trait controls are also matched on minor allele frequency and LD score. Table 1 gives 338 causal variants among 3,380 for Mendelian traits and 1,140 among 11,400 for complex traits. Larger versions with millions of controls per positive are also provided.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Section 4 and Table 1

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Models are scored zero-shot, or by ridge logistic regression on extracted features (linear probing). Linear probing uses one fold per chromosome: each chromosome is tested with a model trained on the others, and the regularisation is tuned by cross-validation on the training chromosomes. The metric is AUPRC per chromosome, averaged across chromosomes with weights by sample size, with a bootstrap standard error. With 9 controls per positive, a random score has AUPRC 0.1. The README names AUPRC_by_chrom_weighted_average as the main metric.

Your own features go in a parquet file under results/dataset/{dataset}/features/, and Snakemake then computes zero-shot or logistic regression metrics for them. A Colab notebook, TraitGym.ipynb, is also offered.

profile.summary: GUANinE v1.1 is a set of large genomic prediction tasks on the human reference genome hg38 and synthetic yeast promoters: chromatin accessibility and regulatory element propensity, sequence conservation, promoter expression, and two variant tasks for deleteriousness (cadd-snv) and pathogenicity (clinvar-snv). Pretrained models are compared with frozen features and a linear probe, scored by Spearman's rho. It suits people comparing supervised sequence-to-function models with genomic language models.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract and Introduction; v1.0 paper Table 1

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Six tasks from v1.0 cover three domains with two tasks each: regulatory element annotation (dnase-propensity, ccre-propensity), sequence conservation (cons30, cons100) and expression of synthetic yeast promoters (gpra-c, gpra-d). Version 1.1 adds cadd-snv, which separates proxy-benign from proxy-deleterious variants, and clinvar-snv, which separates benign from pathogenic noncoding ClinVar variants. The authors say clinvar-snv is a splicing-rich subset of ClinVar, not a test of general pathogenicity.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Introduction; Newly constructed tasks; Table 1 footnote

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: dnase-propensity labels 511 bp hg38 sequences with an ordinal score from 0 (inaccessible) to 4 (almost always accessible), aggregated from over 700 ENCODE SCREEN v2 DHS tracks; ccre-propensity relabels the positive DHSs by four epigenetic marks. cons30 and cons100 label 512 bp segments by binned mean phyloP30 or phyloP100 (0 to 24). gpra-c and gpra-d are 80 bp random yeast promoters labelled by binned fluorescence (0 to 17). cadd-snv uses gnomAD v3 singletons as proxy deleterious and simulated or frequent variants as proxy benign. clinvar-snv has no training set and just under 12 000 variants. Regulatory and variant tasks use chromosome 21 as development and chromosome 22 as test; conservation and yeast tasks use random splits.
sections.source_locator: v1.0 paper: Section 2 and Table 1; v1.1 paper: Table 1 and Newly constructed tasks; docs/tasks/dnase_propensity.rst

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Models are frozen; features are extracted and a linear probe (ridge or logistic regression) is fitted, with the regularisation chosen on the development set before test inference. clinvar-snv has no training set, so models that cannot score zero-shot are calibrated on the development set. Scores are Spearman's rho, reported multiplied by 100 in the documentation example. Most test labels are private; the README says test predictions are submitted through a Google form until an automatic evaluation server launches.

profile.summary: An independent test of 10 deep learning RNA 3D structure predictors on RNA structures released after the methods' training cut-offs. It covers 79 monomeric RNAs and 158 RNA-RNA and RNA-protein complexes, split into easy and hard sets by structural similarity to the training data. It is for structural biologists choosing an RNA structure predictor and wanting to know how far accuracy holds on new folds.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Materials and methods, Benchmark dataset

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether gains reported by RNA structure predictors carry over to RNA structures they could not have seen in training. Ten methods are tested on monomeric RNA; four of them (AF3, Boltz-1, HF3 and RF2NA) are also tested on RNA-RNA and RNA-protein complexes.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Model generation

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: PDB entries released after 30 September 2021 (complexes) and 13 April 2022 (monomers) were downloaded in January 2026, plus RNA-containing CASP16 targets. Sequences were clustered with CD-HIT-EST at 80% identity, both within the set and against PDB RNA deposited before the cut-off. Structures with pairwise TM-score above 0.7 within the set were removed. Complexes with more than four subunits, on which Boltz-1 ran out of memory, were dropped, leaving 158 complexes; the monomer set has 79 structures. Three long monomers (8BU8, 8TVZ, R1248) that DRfold and DeepFoldRNA did not produce were also left out of the main comparison; the text read does not say whether the 79 counts them. Monomers are easy or hard by a 0.5 TM-score cut-off to the PDB training data; a complex is easy if any protein or RNA chain has TM-score of at least 0.7 to a pre-cut-off complex.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Materials and methods, Benchmark dataset and Model generation; Results

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Every method was run with default settings and the same MSAs, generating five models per target; the top-ranked model is scored. Monomers are scored by TM-score (RNA-align), INF, lDDT and GDT-TS; complexes by US-align TM-score, DockQ, F1, fnat, iRMSD and LRMSD. Predictions are trimmed to the residues resolved in the reference. Success rates use CASP16 thresholds, and differences between methods are tested with a Wilcoxon signed-rank test.

profile.summary: A ClinGen Sequence Variant Interpretation calibration that turns missense predictor scores into ACMG/AMP evidence strengths: PP3 (supporting to very strong for pathogenicity) and BP4 (for benignity). Pejaver et al. 2022 calibrated 13 tools on 11,834 ClinVar missense variants using a 4.41% prior from gnomAD; Bergquist et al. 2025 applied the same method to AlphaMissense, ESM1b and VARITY. Clinical laboratories and tool developers use it to set score thresholds for variant classification.
profile.summary_source_locator: Pejaver 2022: Summary, Data sets, Prevalence; Bergquist 2025: Abstract

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: For each tool, the score intervals at which the local posterior probability of pathogenicity, or the local positive likelihood ratio, reaches each ACMG/AMP evidence level. The method estimates a local positive predictive value and can in principle calibrate any continuous score. Bergquist et al. 2025 also map evidence levels to points in the Bayesian adaptation of the guidelines.
sections.source_locator: Pejaver 2022: Summary; Bergquist 2025: Introduction

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The ClinVar 2019 set holds pathogenic, likely pathogenic, likely benign and benign missense variants with gnomAD allele frequency below 0.01, in genes with at least one pathogenic variant; VUS, zero-star and conflicting entries and known training variants of the tools were removed, leaving 11,834 variants in 1,914 genes. The gnomAD set (363,894 variants, 3,640 genes) is used to estimate the prior and how often each evidence level would be assigned; gnomAD variants found in ClinVar were removed. The ClinVar 2020 set (9,114 variants, 2,197 genes) holds variants added after December 2019 and is used for validation.
sections.source_locator: Pejaver 2022: Materials and methods, Data sets

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: The prior probability of pathogenicity was estimated at 4.41% with DistCurve on the gnomAD set. Evidence thresholds correspond to positive likelihood ratios of 2.406, 5.790, 33.53 and 1,124 for supporting, moderate, strong and very strong. A score threshold is set where the one-sided 95% confidence bound of the local likelihood ratio, from 10,000 bootstrap iterations, reaches the required value. Thresholds are then checked on the ClinVar 2020 set. Bergquist et al. 2025 reused the same data sets, parameters and cut-offs.

profile.summary: A small evaluation from the CIViC MCP paper: can a large language model say which CIViC clinical significance labels are supported for a (molecular profile, cancer type, therapy) triplet? GPT-5 was tested alone, with the CIViC MCP server, and in Agent Mode on 100 randomly sampled CIViC triplets. It is relevant to people judging LLM tools for retrieving curated cancer variant evidence; it is one paper's study, not a maintained benchmark.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Section 3

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether an LLM retrieves current CIViC evidence correctly. For each triplet and each candidate clinical significance, the model answers supports, does not support, or no evidence. The authors frame it as a test of retrieval through the MCP server against recall from pretraining or web browsing.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Section 3

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: 100 triplets were randomly selected from CIViC Evidence Items; expected answers come from CIViC. The README describes QA_triplet_dataset.csv as holding the triplets and expected answers. The scoring script reads a CIViC evidence extract dated 2_27_26 in its file name. The illustrative example in the paper was chosen separately and is not in the 100.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Sections 2.1 and 3; README.md: Evaluation Scripts; eval_one_shot.py: CONFIG

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: GPT-5 is prompted zero-shot at temperature 1. Scoring is at the significance-label level, micro-averaged within each Evidence Type, with the common no-evidence label excluded. Reported metrics are overall accuracy and micro-F1, plus mean response time with a 95% confidence interval; the script uses 10,000 bootstrap resamples. The paper reports GPT-5 with MCP at 0.95 accuracy and 0.98 micro-F1, GPT-5 alone at 0.30 and 0.46, and Agent Mode at 0.83 and 0.91.

Clone it at the pinned commit, install the Python requirements, and run eval_one_shot.py from the eval_QA_experiment folder; it rescores the no-MCP, MCP and Agent Mode outputs and writes summary CSVs. profile.summary: The evaluation from the BERTax paper: assign 1,500 nt genome fragments to superkingdom, phylum and, in one dataset, genus. BERTax is compared with Kraken2, sourmash, MMseqs2, minimap2 and DeepMicrobes, all given the same reference or training data, on a closely related split and a genus-held-out split. It is for people choosing a taxonomic classifier, especially for sequences without close relatives in reference databases.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Comparison to Other Classification Approaches

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: How well a method assigns the taxonomic origin of a DNA fragment when close relatives are, or are not, in the reference data. The distantly related dataset simulates unknown sequences by holding out whole genera.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Significance; Three Evaluation Datasets

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Genomes of archaea, eukaryotes, bacteria and viruses were taken from NCBI, and 1 million 1,500 nt fragments per superkingdom were extracted, then clustered at 80% identity. Fine-tuning data keep phyla with at least 10,000 fragments: 30 phylum classes and 2,328,584 samples. The closely related dataset tests on 2,000 random samples per phylum; the distantly related dataset tests on whole held-out genera, balanced to 1,780 samples per phylum; the final model dataset adds 2 million eukaryotic and bacterial fragments and has 5 superkingdom, 44 phylum and 156 genus classes, split like the closely related dataset. In every case 95% of the rest is training and 5% validation.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods, Data, Pretraining Dataset, Preparing Data for Fine-Tuning, Three Evaluation Datasets

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Each tool is scored by macro average precision (AveP) at superkingdom and phylum, and at genus for the final dataset. Database tools get only the training partition as reference, default parameters are used, and MMseqs2 is also run with taxonomy parameters to obtain a confidence for precision-recall curves. DeepMicrobes is trained on the same data. The share of sequences each tool classifies is reported alongside, since database tools leave some unclassified.

profile.summary: The variant effect benchmarks used in the GPN-MSA paper to test unsupervised deleteriousness scores on the human genome. They pit ClinVar pathogenic, COSMIC frequent and OMIM regulatory variants against common gnomAD variants, test enrichment of rare over common gnomAD variants among the most deleterious scores, and add ProteinGym DMS and DepMap gene essentiality. They are for comparing DNA language models with conservation scores, CADD and protein models on coding and non-coding variants.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Methods, Main VEP metrics

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether a score ranks deleterious human variants above neutral ones without being trained on human variant labels. Coding variants are tested through ClinVar, COSMIC and DMS; non-coding through OMIM regulatory variants and gnomAD; gene-level through DepMap essentiality.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Results

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: ClinVar release 20230730; COSMIC MutantCensus v98 with frequency computed from whole-genome or whole-exome samples; a curated OMIM set of pathogenic regulatory variants; gnomAD 3.1.2 filtered to allele number of at least 25000 with common variants above 5% MAF and rare variants as singletons; ProteinGym v0.1 human DMS data; DepMap Public 23Q4 gene dependency. OMIM variants are matched to gnomAD common variants by regulatory category. The ablation set subsamples rare variants to match common variants per consequence. The labelled ClinVar, COSMIC, OMIM and gnomAD sets are published on Hugging Face.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, VEP data sources, Main and Additional VEP metrics; docs/models/gpn-msa.md

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Each method gives one score per variant (for GPN-MSA, the log-likelihood ratio of alternate to reference, averaged over strands). ClinVar is scored by AUROC; COSMIC, OMIM and DepMap by AUPRC; gnomAD by the odds ratio of rare to common variants in the deleterious tail, with the tail set by allowing about 30 false discoveries and p-values from a one-sided Fisher's exact test. DMS sets are binarised with ProteinGym cut-offs, except TADBP, where a 0.125 cut-off on absolute relative toxicity is used. Some expensive models were scored only on ClinVar or part of OMIM.

profile.summary: DNALONGBENCH is five DNA prediction tasks that need long input sequences, up to about 1 million base pairs: enhancer-target gene pairs, eQTLs, 3D chromatin contact maps, regulatory sequence activity and base-pair transcription initiation signals. Each task compares a task-specific expert model, a CNN and fine-tuned DNA foundation models (HyenaDNA, Caduceus-Ph, Caduceus-PS). It is for developers testing whether long-context DNA models capture long-range dependencies.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether a model can use long DNA context for problems where distant sequence matters: linking enhancers to target genes, flagging eQTLs, predicting chromatin contacts, predicting thousands of epigenomic tracks, and predicting transcription initiation at base-pair resolution.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Results, Proposed dataset

sections.title: Enhancer-target gene and eQTL tasks
sections.body: Enhancer-target gene pairs are CRISPRi-validated enhancer-promoter interactions in K562 cells from three studies, kept within 450 kb of the TSS; 2,602 samples, scored by AUROC. The eQTL task adapts Enformer's SuSiE fine-mapped eQTL set for the top nine tissues, keeps candidates within 450 kb of the TSS, masks other variants in each interval, and splits 8:1:1 by stratified random sampling; 31,282 samples, scored by AUROC.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods; README.md: Data Download table

sections.title: Contact map, regulatory activity and transcription initiation tasks
sections.body: Contact maps use Akita's processed data for five cell lines plus four more from the 4DN portal, 1 Mbp inputs at 2 kb bins, split by random virtual contigs 8:1:1 into 7008, 419 and 413 sequences, scored by SCC and PCC. Regulatory activity uses Enformer's 5313 human and 1643 mouse tracks, with 1937 human and 2017 mouse test sequences, scored by PCC averaged over test samples. Transcription initiation uses Puffin's data for five assays on both strands, evaluated on test chromosomes 8 and 9 by PCC.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Each task reuses processed data from earlier studies (CRISPRi screens, Akita, Enformer, Puffin) and provides inputs as BED coordinates so flanking context can be changed. The datasets are deposited on Harvard Dataverse.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Results; Data availability

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Models are trained or fine-tuned on each task's training split and scored on its test set with the task's metric: AUROC for the two classification tasks, SCC and PCC for contact maps, PCC for the two regression tasks. Foundation models feed sequence features to linear heads; for eQTL, reference and alternate representations are combined before a classifier. The paper reports that expert models scored highest on every task.

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: Create the conda environment, clone the repository and install the package, download a task's data from Dataverse, then run the CNN baseline's train.py for that task; the script trains, saves the best validation checkpoint to best_model.pt, and prints the test metric for the final-epoch model, not the saved checkpoint.
